claims.text: Laboratory-scale spark plasma sintering can be used to fabricate ZrB2 specimens.
High-pressure SPS at approximately 1600–1650 °C can fully densify submicrometer ZrB2 powder.
The proposed low-temperature SPS process will retain a single-phase ZrB2 microstructure with minimal secondary phases.
The proposed SPS process will produce uniformly dense ZrB2 with submicrometer grains.
Rapid heating at at least 100 °C/min and a 5–10 minute dwell will limit grain growth in ZrB2.
High pressure during SPS enhances mass transport sufficiently to enable lower-temperature densification of ZrB2.
A refined ZrB2 microstructure will form a more stable and protective oxide scale.
A fine, dense ZrB2 microstructure will minimize penetration paths for corrosive liquid plating metal.
The proposed SPS-processed ZrB2 will have oxidation resistance superior to conventionally sintered and prior lower-temperature ZrB2.
The proposed SPS-processed ZrB2 will have lower liquid-plating-metal corrosion than conventionally sintered and prior lower-temperature ZrB2.
The proposed SPS-processed ZrB2 will maintain strength comparable to or greater than the controls.
Traditional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Earlier lower-temperature ZrB2 routes generally still require temperatures above 1700 °C.
Conventionally sintered and earlier lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens have coarse grains.
Conventionally sintered and earlier lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens have incomplete densification or residual porosity.
The baseline ZrB2 specimens are vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation.
The baseline ZrB2 specimens are vulnerable to liquid-metal corrosion.
Density, hardness, and oxidation measurements have previously been performed on SPS-fabricated ZrB2 benchmark specimens.
Vickers microhardness is an adequate measure of the mechanical strength predicted by the hypothesis.
The proposed material will remain effective during high-temperature oxidizing exposure and immersion in liquid plating-metal baths.
